The Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara are three peoples of the upper Missouri River in North Dakota, who now form one nation, the Three Affiliated Tribes. For centuries they lived in fortified villages of round earth lodges on the river bluffs, growing maize, beans, squash and sunflowers and hunting bison.

Their villages were great trading centres, where Plains peoples brought horses and hides to trade for corn, and later for European goods. The Lewis and Clark expedition spent the winter of 1804 to 1805 at Fort Mandan nearby, where they met Sacagawea, a Shoshone woman living among the Hidatsa.

A smallpox epidemic in 1837 killed most of the Mandan. The survivors of the three peoples came together at Like-a-Fishhook Village in 1845 and later on the Fort Berthold Reservation. In the 1950s the Garrison Dam flooded their best river land under Lake Sakakawea. See also Mandan and Arikara.
